claim: Satiety-signaling, pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus play a pivotal role in the regulation of energy homeostasis.
source: Satiety-signaling, pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC)-expressing neurons in the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus play a pivotal role in the regulation of energy homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract and introduction, supported by the broader scientific literature on POMC neurons.

claim: Recent studies reported altered mitochondrial dynamics in POMC neurons during diet-induced obesity.
source: Recent studies reported altered mitochondrial dynamics and decreased mitochondria- endoplasmic reticulum contacts in POMC neurons during diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings, specifically citing work by Schneeberger et al., 2013 in the introduction.

claim: Recent studies reported decreased mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum contacts in POMC neurons during diet-induced obesity.
source: Recent studies reported altered mitochondrial dynamics and decreased mitochondria- endoplasmic reticulum contacts in POMC neurons during diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This claim references prior research findings, specifically citing work by Schneeberger et al., 2013 in the introduction.

claim: In diet-induced obesity, cellular Ca2+ handling properties including mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake capacity are impaired.
source: In diet-induced obesity, cellular Ca2+ handling properties including mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake capacity are impaired, and an increased resting level of free intracellular Ca2+ is accompanied by a marked decrease in neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In diet-induced obesity, an increased resting level of free intracellular Ca2+ is accompanied by a marked decrease in neuronal excitability in POMC neurons.
source: In diet-induced obesity, cellular Ca2+ handling properties including mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake capacity are impaired, and an increased resting level of free intracellular Ca2+ is accompanied by a marked decrease in neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Experimentally increasing intracellular Ca2+ concentrations reproduced electrophysiological properties observed in diet-induced obesity.
source: Experimentally increasing or decreasing intracellular Ca2+ concentrations reproduced electrophysiological properties observed in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 5-8.

claim: Experimentally decreasing intracellular Ca2+ concentrations reproduced electrophysiological properties observed in diet-induced obesity.
source: Experimentally increasing or decreasing intracellular Ca2+ concentrations reproduced electrophysiological properties observed in diet-induced obesity.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 5-8.

claim: The study provides the first direct evidence for a diet-dependent deterioration of Ca2+ homeostasis in POMC neurons during obesity development.
source: Taken together, we provide the first direct evidence for a diet-dependent deterioration of Ca2+ homeostasis in POMC neurons during obesity development resulting in impaired function of these critical energy homeostasis-regulating neurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Diet-dependent deterioration of Ca2+ homeostasis in POMC neurons results in impaired function of these critical energy homeostasis-regulating neurons.
source: Taken together, we provide the first direct evidence for a diet-dependent deterioration of Ca2+ homeostasis in POMC neurons during obesity development resulting in impaired function of these critical energy homeostasis-regulating neurons.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations to Apovian, 2016; Gao and Horvath, 2007; Power, 2012.

claim: Hypothalamic control circuits adapt food intake and energy expenditure to the needs of the organism and the availability of fuel sources in the periphery of the body.

claim: Dysregulation of hypothalamic functional circuitry can cause metabolic disorders including obesity and type two diabetes.

claim: In anorexigenic POMC neurons, diet-induced obesity decreased mitochondria-ER contacts by downregulation of MFN2.

claim: Increased Ca2+ load on the cell can result in impaired neuronal function.

claim: Diet-induced obesity impaired intracellular Ca2+ handling in POMC neurons, including mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake.
source: We found that diet-induced obesity impaired intracellular Ca2+ handling, including mitochondrial Ca2+ uptake.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The changes in Ca2+ handling in POMC neurons were accompanied by a marked decrease in activity and excitability.
source: The changes in Ca2+ handling were accompanied by a marked decrease in activity and excitability of POMC neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Mice exposed to 11–13 weeks of HFD-feeding (starting at an age of 6 weeks) showed an elevation in body weight compared to NCD-fed controls.
source: Mice exposed to 11–13 weeks of HFD-feeding (starting at an age of 6 weeks) showed an elevation in body weight (control: 29.3 ± 1.9 g, n = 25; DIO: 38.6 ± 4.1 g, n = 25; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental measurements.

claim: Mice exposed to 11–13 weeks of HFD-feeding (starting at an age of 6 weeks) showed an elevation in body fat content compared to NCD-fed controls.
source: and body fat content (control: 12.7 ± 4.2%, n = 25; DIO: 32.1 ± 4.0%, n = 25; p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test) compared to NCD-fed controls.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental measurements.

claim: The activity of POMC neurons of mice exposed to a HFD was clearly reduced.
source: The activity of POMC neurons of mice exposed to a HFD was clearly reduced, which is in line with previous results (Jo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data in Figure 1, and consistent with prior literature.

claim: The membrane potential of POMC neurons was hyperpolarized in DIO mice compared to control mice.
source: The membrane potential was hyperpolarized (Figure 1A,B; control: −58.8 ± 1.1 mV, n = 26; DIO: −64.0 ± 1.2 mV, n = 37; p=0.0046, Mann-Whitney test)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The spontaneous activity of POMC neurons was decreased in DIO mice compared to control mice.
source: and the spontaneous activity was decreased (Figure 1A,C; control: 3.4 ± 0.7 Hz, n = 26; DIO: 1.7 ± 0.4 Hz, n = 37; p=0.037, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1A,C.

claim: The percentage of POMC neurons without spontaneous action potential firing increased from 31% in control mice to 51% in DIO mice.
source: Moreover, the percentage of POMC neurons without spontaneous action potential firing (NSAN, not spontaneously active neuron; F < 0.5 Hz) increased from 31% (8 of 26) in control mice to 51% (19 of 37) in DIO mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: The number of POMC neurons with strong spike frequency adaptation was markedly enhanced in DIO mice.
source: Likewise, the number of POMC neurons with strong spike frequency adaptation was markedly enhanced, i.e., the percentage of neurons with a spike frequency adaptation ratio (SFA, for details see Materials and methods) >3 increased from 21% (4 of 19) in the control group to 34% (10 of 29) in the DIO group (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Previous studies reported changes in glutamatergic synaptic innervation of POMC neurons during a sustained HFD.
source: Previous studies reported changes in both glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic innervation of POMC neurons during a sustained HFD (Klöckener et al., 2011; Newton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: Previous studies reported changes in GABAergic synaptic innervation of POMC neurons during a sustained HFD.
source: Previous studies reported changes in both glutamatergic and GABAergic synaptic innervation of POMC neurons during a sustained HFD (Klöckener et al., 2011; Newton et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: The observed hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in POMC neurons was not caused by changes in synaptic input.
source: Since all our experiments were performed in the presence of ionotropic synaptic blockers (for details see Materials and methods), it is unlikely that the observed hyperpolarization of the membrane potential in POMC neurons was caused by changes in synaptic input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design (use of synaptic blockers).

claim: The inhibitory postsynaptic current frequency was increased in DIO.
source: Whole-cell voltage-clamp recordings revealed that the inhibitory postsynaptic current frequency was increased in DIO.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Application of picrotoxin and CGP54626 blocked GABAergic currents and eliminated IPSCs completely.
source: Application of picrotoxin (100 µM), a GABAA receptor antagonist, and CGP54626 (50 µM), a GABAB receptor antagonist, blocked GABAergic currents and eliminated IPSCs completely (data not shown).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data.

claim: Neither picrotoxin nor CGP54626 restored the membrane potential and firing rate to control levels in DIO POMC neurons.
source: However, neither picrotoxin nor CGP54626 restored the membrane potential and firing rate to control levels (Figure 1F; PTX: n = 12, p=0.3590; CGP: n = 6; p=0.2052; paired t-tests).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F.

claim: The DIO-induced hyperpolarization and the decrease in firing rate cannot be exclusively attributed to the increase in inhibitory input organization of POMC neurons.
source: The results show that the DIO-induced hyperpolarization and the decrease in firing rate cannot be exclusively attributed to the increase in inhibitory input organization of these cells, but are also a consequence of altered cell-intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that GABA receptor blockers did not restore normal activity.

claim: The DIO-induced hyperpolarization and the decrease in firing rate are a consequence of altered cell-intrinsic properties of POMC neurons.
source: The results show that the DIO-induced hyperpolarization and the decrease in firing rate cannot be exclusively attributed to the increase in inhibitory input organization of these cells, but are also a consequence of altered cell-intrinsic properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing that GABA receptor blockers did not restore normal activity.

claim: POMC neurons without spontaneous activity had a two-fold higher SFA ratio than spontaneously firing POMC neurons.
source: Overall, we found that POMC neurons without spontaneous activity had a two-fold higher SFA ratio than spontaneously firing POMC neurons (Figure 2A–C; POMC firing: 2.0 ± 0.1, n = 27; POMC silent: 3.6 ± 0.3, n = 22, p<0.0001, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A–C.

claim: Silent POMC neurons showed a strong reduction of the action potential number over the time course of the depolarizing stimulus compared to spontaneously firing POMC neurons.
source: This was particularly reflected in a strong reduction of the action potential number over the time course of the depolarizing stimulus (Figure 2D; POMC firing: 188 ± 10, n = 25; POMC silent: 130 ± 11.0, n = 22; p=0.0009, Mann-Whitney test).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D.

claim: In DIO mice, the excitability of anorexigenic POMC neurons is markedly reduced.
source: Collectively, these data show that in DIO mice, the excitability of anorexigenic POMC neurons is markedly reduced.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Increased levels of free intracellular Ca2+ were found in POMC neurons in DIO compared to control mice.
source: Surprisingly, these experiments revealed increased levels of free intracellular Ca2+ in POMC neurons in DIO compared to control mice (Figure 3A; control: 19.3 ± 2.3 nM, n = 11; DIO: 45.8 ± 7.3 nM, n = 13; p=0.0007, Mann-Whitney test)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: The increased levels of free intracellular Ca2+ in DIO POMC neurons was not expected because of the DIO-induced hyperpolarization and decreased activity of the neurons.
source: which was not expected, because of the DIO-induced hyperpolarization and decreased activity of the neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the unexpected finding.

claim: The endogenous Ca2+-binding ratio was reduced in POMC neurons of DIO mice compared to control mice.
source: Using this method, we found that the endogenous Ca2+-binding ratio (Figure 3F; control: 497 ± 18; DIO: 240 ± 5; p=0.0001, unpaired t-test)
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3F.

claim: The Ca2+ extrusion rate was reduced in POMC neurons of DIO mice compared to control mice.
source: and, simultaneously, the Ca2+ extrusion rate (Figure 3G; control: 150 ± 3 s−1; DIO: 111 ± 1 s−1; p<0.0001; unpaired t-test) were reduced in POMC neurons of DIO mice compared to control mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3G.

claim: Mitochondria play a crucial role in intracellular Ca2+ handling.
source: Since mitochondria play a crucial role in intracellular Ca2+ handling, we investigated whether the mitochondrial capacity of POMC neurons to accumulate Ca2+ was affected in DIO mice (Santo-Domingo and Demaurex, 2010; Szabadkai and Duchen, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, supported by citations.

claim: FCCP induced a lower elevation of free cytosolic Ca2+ in DIO POMC neurons than in control POMC neurons.
source: FCCP induced a lower elevation of free cytosolic Ca2+ in the DIO (Δ F340/F380 = 0.012 ± 0.001, n = 72 cells, N = 11 brain slices) than in the control cohort (Δ F340/F380 = 0.020 ± 0.003, n = 46 cells, N = 10 brain slices) (Figure 4B,C; p=0.0406, unpaired t-test).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The lower FCCP-induced elevation of free cytosolic Ca2+ in DIO POMC neurons indicates a reduced mitochondrial capacity to accumulate Ca2+.
source: This indicates a reduced mitochondrial capacity to accumulate Ca2+ in POMC neurons of DIO mice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Elevating extracellular Ca2+ concentrations from 2 mM to 4 mM increased intracellular Ca2+ levels in POMC neurons.
source: Elevating extracellular Ca2+ concentrations from 2 mM to 4 mM increased intracellular Ca2+ levels and decreased the hyperpolarizing holding current (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Elevating extracellular Ca2+ concentrations from 2 mM to 4 mM decreased the hyperpolarizing holding current in POMC neurons.
source: Elevating extracellular Ca2+ concentrations from 2 mM to 4 mM increased intracellular Ca2+ levels and decreased the hyperpolarizing holding current (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ caused a drop in free intracellular Ca2+ in POMC neurons.
source: In contrast, reducing extracellular Ca2+ caused a drop in free intracellular Ca2+, increased the hyperpolarizing holding current, and even induced the generation of action potentials (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ increased the hyperpolarizing holding current in POMC neurons.
source: In contrast, reducing extracellular Ca2+ caused a drop in free intracellular Ca2+, increased the hyperpolarizing holding current, and even induced the generation of action potentials (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Reducing extracellular Ca2+ induced the generation of action potentials in POMC neurons.
source: In contrast, reducing extracellular Ca2+ caused a drop in free intracellular Ca2+, increased the hyperpolarizing holding current, and even induced the generation of action potentials (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5A–C.

claim: Reducing intracellular Ca2+ depolarized the membrane potential in silent POMC neurons.
source: As hypothesized, reducing intracellular Ca2+ depolarized the membrane potential and led to the generation of spontaneous action potentials in silent POMC neurons (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Reducing intracellular Ca2+ led to the generation of spontaneous action potentials in silent POMC neurons.
source: As hypothesized, reducing intracellular Ca2+ depolarized the membrane potential and led to the generation of spontaneous action potentials in silent POMC neurons (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6A,C.

claim: Increasing intracellular Ca2+ reduced the action potential frequency in neurons that were spontaneously active.
source: Increasing intracellular Ca2+ reduced the action potential frequency in neurons that were spontaneously active (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6B,D.

claim: Removing extracellular Ca2+ did not change the intrinsic electrophysiological properties of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells of rats.
source: It is important to note that this is not a general effect, that is, removing extracellular Ca2+ did not change the intrinsic electrophysiological properties of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells of rats (Penn et al., 2016; Su et al., 2001).
